deep.reconstruction:
The page continues Gauss's table 'Gemeine Brüche in Decimalbrüche verwandelt' from the previous folio. For each prime denominator p (the 'Nenner'), he writes out the full decimal periods of a/p, one for each coset of the subgroup <10> in (Z/pZ)*. This is the working material for the method of Disquisitiones Arithmeticae Art. 312-318. A fraction a/p can be read off by rotating the right period. The underlined leading digits serve as an index for finding that rotation.

Each period below is 'the numerator a, with an expansion whose digits D form the repeating block'. In modern notation each entry is a*(10^e - 1)/p = D, where e = ord_p(10).

(1) p = 167. Here ord_167(10) = 166 = p-1, so 10 is a primitive root and a single period suffices.
- Reason (mine): 2 is a quadratic residue because 167 ≡ 7 mod 8. 5 is a non-residue because (5/167) = (2/5) = -1. So 10 is a non-residue, and its order is 166.
- He writes the 166 digits of 100/167 = 0.598802395...149700, then repeats '598802395 &c'.
- Equivalently, 1/167 = 0.00598802...
- The digit count is 40+40+42+41+3 = 166.

(2) p = 199. Here ord_199(10) = 99 = (p-1)/2, so 10 generates the quadratic residues and two periods are needed.
- Reason (mine): 2 is a residue since 199 ≡ 7 mod 8, and (5/199) = (4/5) = 1, so 10 is a residue.
- First block: 100/199 = 0.502512562814...020100, then the repeat 5025125 (underlined). The digit count is 99+7.
- Second block: 21/199 = 0.1055276381909...44221, then the repeat 105527638 (underlined). The digit count is 99+9.
- 21 is the least numerator a > 19.9 (so that a/p starts with a nonzero digit) lying in the non-residue coset. Check (mine): (3/199) = -1 and (7/199) = +1.

(3) p = 73. Here ord_73(10) = 8, so there are 72/8 = 9 cosets, each with an 8-digit period. The 3-digit index after each period is floor(1000a/73):
- 10/73 = .13698630 (136)
- 8/73 = .10958904 (109)
- 9/73 = .12328767 (123)
- 11/73 = .15068493 (150)
- 12/73 = .16438356 (164)
- 13/73 = .17808219 (178)
- 15/73 = .20547945 (205)
- 19/73 = .26027397 (260)
- 18/73 = .24657534 (246)

Each numerator is the least element above 7.3 in its coset. Two entries in the third row are struck out, presumably duplicates or false starts. A marginal note under 73, apparently Latin, is not securely legible.

(4) p = 127. Here ord_127(10) = 42, so the index is 3 and the cosets are those of the cubic residues.
- Reason (mine): 10^3 ≡ -16 and 10^6 ≡ 2, so 10^21 ≡ -1 and 10^42 ≡ 1.
- Three 42-digit periods are written:
  - 100/127 = .787401574803149606299212598425196850393700 (bracket [787)
  - 13/127 = .102362204724409448818897637795275590551181 (index 1023)
  - 17/127 = .133858267716535433070866141732283464566929 (index 13385)
- The numerators (13) and (17) are noted in the margin. A struck-out third attempt appears between them.

(5) p = 131. Here ord_131(10) = 130 = p-1, giving a single period.
- 100/131 = .763358 778625 954198 ... 068702 2900, followed by the repeat 7633587, written in groups of six.
- Midy's property checks: digit k + digit k+65 = 9.

(6) p = 137. Here ord_137(10) = 8, because 10^4 ≡ -1 (137·73 = 10001). That gives 17 cosets.
- Periods are listed with a 2-digit index floor(100a/137):
  - a = 100 (index 72), written 72992700 72
  - a = 14, 15 (index 10), 16 (11), 17 (12), 18 (13), 20 (14), 21 (15), 22 (16), 24 (17)
  - a = 27 (19), 28 (20), 31 (22), 32 (23), 35 (25), 42 (30), 48 (35)
- I verified (mine) that these 17 numerators represent all 17 cosets of <10> = {1,10,100,41,136,127,37,96} with no repeats. Apart from the first coset, each representative is the least coset element above 13.7.

Purpose: this is the computational basis of Gauss's table for converting any fraction with prime denominator into a decimal. Only one period per coset is stored, and the leading digits locate the starting point.
errors: No numerical errors found: all checked periods (100/167, 100/199, 21/199, the nine 73-periods, the three 127-periods, 100/131, the seventeen 137-periods) agree with the true expansions; the struck-out entries (73, rows 3; 127, middle row) are Gauss's own corrections and the final entries are correct.

results.what: Full decimal periods of 1/p for p = 167, 131 (10 a primitive root) with period length p-1
results.modern_name: Full reptend primes / decimal period = multiplicative order of 10 mod p
results.usually_credited_to: Known in the 18th century (Wallis, J. H. Lambert, Robertson); systematic theory in Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801) Art. 312-318

results.what: When ord_p(10) = (p-1)/k, store k periods, one per coset of <10> in (Z/p)*, chosen with numerator just above p/10, and indexed by leading digits (p = 199, 73, 127, 137)
results.modern_name: Coset decomposition of (Z/pZ)* by the subgroup generated by 10; Gauss's table for converting fractions to decimals
results.usually_credited_to: C. F. Gauss, Disq. Arith. Art. 314-317; the table is printed posthumously in Werke II (1863)

deep.surprise_reason: This is working material for Gauss's well-known table of decimal periods (Disq. Arith. Art. 312-318; Werke II). It is computationally impressive but contains no new results.

checkable.asserts: Period lengths of the decimal expansions for the six denominators
Gauss's 166-digit period for 167 equals the period of 100/167
21 lies in the non-residue coset not reached by powers of 10

checkable.sympy: len(set(frozenset((a*pow(10,k,73))%73 for k in range(8)) for a in [10,8,9,11,12,13,15,19,18]))==9
checkable.asserts: The nine numerators represent distinct cosets of <10> mod 73

checkable.sympy: len(set(frozenset((a*pow(10,k,127))%127 for k in range(42)) for a in [1,13,17]))==3
checkable.asserts: 1, 13, 17 represent the three cosets of <10> mod 127
Gauss's 130-digit period for 131 equals the period of 100/131
The 17 numerators exhaust the cosets of <10> in (Z/137)*

transcription_corrections: Title: 'Gemeine Brüche in Decimalbrüchen'. 'Math 17' is a later archival shelf-mark, and '16' is the folio number.
Row 137: '7299270072' is the period 72992700 followed by the underlined index 72 (from a = 100), not a 10-digit period.

Row 199: '1055276381909547738693467336683417085 42' should read continuously '105527638190954773869346733668341708542'. The underlined tails '5025125' and '105527638' are repetitions marking the period end.
Row 127: '(13)' and '(17)' in the margin are the numerators of the second and third periods. '[787' marks the first period (numerator 100).
Row 73: the marginal note under 73 is an illegible (probably Latin) remark, not a number. The struck entries in row 3, columns 1 and 3, are deletions.
Row 131: the last group reads '290076 33587' (period ends ...2900, then the repeat 7633587).
